description:
We're building SPHEREx Drift for the "Planet X and SPHEREx". It already works on real data for all five test targets. It adds WISE images back to 2010 for a 16-year baseline, measures an object's motion straight from the images and checks it against the catalogue, plots spectra and light curves, and lets you hide a simulated "Planet X" in real images to see whether you could spot it.

 Our skills are web development (Next.js, TypeScript), Python and working with astronomical image data.
summary: SPHEREx Drift helps people see what moves and changes in the infrared sky. It combines real WISE observations across years with SPHEREx DR1 spectral mosaics in a public browser app. Blink playback, coloured motion trails and difference images make changes easier to inspect; a motion finder measures candidate tracks, while spectra connect a selected sky position to its infrared brightness across wavelengths. In live testing, it recovered WISE 0855 moving west at about 8.2 arcseconds per year across 23 observing dates. Five prepared fields let judges and learners explore real observations without waiting for an external archive search.
details:
The problem

A moving or variable object can look ordinary in a single sky image. Finding the change requires comparing observations of the same location, keeping their alignment consistent, and understanding what the different dates and wavelengths represent. Those steps can be a barrier for students and citizen scientists who want to explore public infrared observations without first setting up an astronomy software environment. SPHEREx alone returns about 3,600 images a day, and NASA's first SPHEREx brown-dwarf study analysed 37 objects while noting thousands more awaiting analysis.

The solution

SPHEREx Drift brings that comparison into a browser. Users can select Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae or R Draconis, or enter coordinates or an object name. The viewer provides three complementary ways to inspect the field:

  • Blink plays the observing dates in sequence.
  • Trail assigns colours across time (blue = oldest, orange = newest) so motion stands out in a single picture.
  • Difference subtracts comparable images to separate changing sources from the static background.

The timeline and frame thumbnails keep the observations accessible. Users can change the field of view, wavelength band, image stretch and playback settings, then share the current view through its URL. The same viewer works on desktop and mobile.

How it works

  1. Fetch real archive pixels. WISE: time-resolved unWISE images accessed through the WiseView service, keeping the observing dates needed for motion analysis. SPHEREx: calibrated DR1 all-sky spectral cube cutouts with their original wavelength tables.
  2. Align. The Python backend reprojects every image onto a common grid with north up and east left.
  3. Show change. The browser renders Blink, Trail and Difference views on a canvas, with band views across the six SPHEREx detectors.
  4. Measure. The motion finder searches for straight-line tracks across multiple dates; the Spectrum panel reads calibrated SPHEREx surface brightness at a selected position; the Brightness panel gives relative WISE trends for variable stars.
  5. Give context. Gaia DR3 positions and proper-motion arrows, survey reference images and catalogue links help users investigate the surrounding field.

The five preset fields include prepared copies of real observations, with source URLs and checksums, so the demonstration keeps working when the external archive-search service is unavailable. Other positions use live services.

Results

On WISE 0855 the motion finder recovered a westward motion of about 8.2 arcseconds per year over 23 WISE observing dates, against a catalogued value of about 8.1. This is a demonstration on a known moving source, not a claim of a new discovery. The deployed app passed 17 real-data browser acceptance checks (all five targets, spectra, six wavelength bands, playback modes, motion recovery, brightness trends, mobile use, accessibility and error checks) and 82 unit and regression tests.

Scientific limits

The prepared SPHEREx DR1 mosaics combine observations and have 12.9-arcsecond native pixels. They provide spectral context rather than separate observing epochs; the time-resolved demonstrations use WISE. Blank and masked spectral channels are excluded. For bright targets with unusable cores, an outer-halo measurement is labelled as such. WISE brightness trends are quick-look measurements, not precision photometry. Candidate tracks require further investigation, and a feature marker on the spectrum is not a confirmed chemical detection. Asteroid matching is unavailable for mosaics because it needs individual exposure dates. An optional injected-object simulation is clearly labelled and never presented as an observation.

Impact and next steps

The prototype lets a learner move from a familiar star field to evidence of motion, brightness changes and wavelength-dependent emission within one interface: a visible change leads to a measured candidate and then to its observational context, with sources and limitations kept visible. Next steps are to expand prepared field coverage, add persistent caching for arbitrary positions, strengthen quality and saturation handling, and extend the time-resolved SPHEREx experience as archive access and data releases develop. Data access is separated from viewing and analysis so new releases can be added without rebuilding the interface.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript and the browser Canvas API. Backend: Python FastAPI with Astropy, astropy-healpix, NumPy, SciPy, reproject, Photutils, Pillow and HTTPX. Hosting: Vercel. Testing: Vitest, pytest, Playwright (against the deployed app with real data) and axe-core accessibility checks.

Use of AI (SI) tools

AI assistance was used during development. OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT and CommandCode (model identifier deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-fast) assisted with application code, debugging, tests, deployment troubleshooting, research and documentation. Anthropic Claude Code assisted with research and produced the demo video edit: it captured the live app with Playwright, composed titles and captions with Remotion, and trimmed pauses and reduced noise in the narration. The narration is the team owner's own recorded voice, and the app footage consists of screen captures of the deployed app. OpenAI ImageGen produced AI-edited screenshot concepts for a possible team avatar; these are presentation assets, not observations. The live scientific views use real WISE and SPHEREx archive pixels processed with numerical algorithms. No AI model creates the observation arrays, fills masked measurements or performs the live motion detection.
